mechanisms.problemSolved: A marketing hero above a product inserts a screen of scrolling between wanting the object and being able to buy it; a category band above the fold costs the first row of products.
mechanisms.mechanism: States the requirement as an outcome, not an arrangement: on a product surface the object and the means of acquiring it are apprehensible together; on a listing the products start on the first screen.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Stated as an outcome it constrains nothing visual, so the arrangement stays a direction decision while the buyer never pays a scroll to reach the control.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: floor/buy.md, opening obligation. Keep lines 46-47; drop the 49-52 rationale, which argues by contrast with a deleted marketing mode and pins a 200px band.

A two-column drawing-sheet layout, object left, spec-and-buy panel right
A dense tabular catalogue row whose price cell and buy cell are in the same row, with no product page at all

mechanisms.problemSolved: A price the buyer has to search for is read as a price being hidden.
mechanisms.mechanism: The price is locatable without search on every surface the object appears on. Stated as an outcome; the file's own type-rank answer (second-largest type) is the appearance form and is discarded.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Findability is a perceptual property with many solutions, so it can be met by position, by weight, by repetition or by language, none of which imply the others.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: floor/buy.md. Replace 'price is the second-largest type on the page' with the outcome.

Price in a fixed column position in a table, identical on every row
Price spoken in a configurator's running sentence: 'this configuration, 14 200 kr'

mechanisms.problemSolved: Delivery cost, delivery time and return terms discovered inside checkout are the classic abandonment cause; the buyer commits to a number and then finds the real number.
mechanisms.mechanism: Everything the buyer will actually pay and wait for is legible at the moment of commitment without navigating away. Logistics stated before checkout, never inside it.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: It ties disclosure to a moment rather than to a container, so any layout that reaches the moment satisfies it. 'A buyer should never scroll to check what they are about to pay' is the strongest line in the source file.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: floor/buy.md, purchase obligations. Keep line 164's sentence; drop 'inside the panel' from 162-163.
threeRenditions: One panel holding price, variant, delivery cost and time beside the control
A running summary bar that restates the total as choices are made
A confirm step that restates the whole commitment on its own page before anything is charged

mechanisms.problemSolved: When the acquire control has the same weight as three other controls, the buyer hesitates over which one commits them.
mechanisms.mechanism: Exactly one control on the surface acquires the object and it cannot be confused with any other control. Secondary actions are secondary and look it.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: The obligation is distinguishability, which is achievable by fill, by isolation, by size, by position or by containment. The source file spent it on colour reservation, which is one rendition and the one that made three shops identical.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: floor/buy.md. State as distinguishability and explicitly forbid colour reservation as the default answer, naming it as one option among several.
threeRenditions: It is the only filled control among outlines
It is the only control inside the purchase panel; everything else on the page is a text link
It is set apart by a rule with nothing else in its band, at any weight

mechanisms.problemSolved: A buyer who decides while reading the specification has to scroll back up to act, and some do not.
mechanisms.mechanism: From any point where the buyer might decide, the purchase control is reachable without hunting.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Reachability is the obligation; stickiness is one implementation. NORDRIG-AB-FORENSICS.md:37-38 shows 'sticky buy panel, mobile bottom bar' listed as a line item in build B's method, which is precisely how a floor rule became a visual signature.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Six specs shown when twelve exist: the buyer who cares finds out and reads the omission as concealment.
mechanisms.mechanism: Every specification that exists is shown. Group them if there are many; never curate the set.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: An omitted spec reads as a hidden one, and the buyer most likely to complete is the one who reads specs. Completeness is a content property, entirely independent of presentation.

mechanisms.problemSolved: A mean rating with no count and no negatives is indistinguishable from a filtered one, and buyers correctly assume it is filtered.

mechanisms.problemSolved: An empty proof slot invites fabrication, and a buyer is one search away from checking.
mechanisms.mechanism: Where proof does not exist, its absence is stated plainly with the reason. It is never manufactured.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Naming the absence converts a suspicious gap into a disclosed fact, and it removes the pressure that produces invented reviews. It is the commerce instance of SKILL.md:157-159 ('when you need the sentence and lack the fact, ask for it or cut the sentence').

mechanisms.problemSolved: A number that animates is a number the buyer re-checks; motion near a price reads as the price being manipulated.
mechanisms.mechanism: Nothing animates on a price, in the basket, or at checkout.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: It is a prohibition rather than a prescription, so it constrains no look at all while removing a specific trust failure.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: floor/buy.md. Drop the two-item allowlist and the '--motion-fast' token name at line 104 — a token from one design system has no business in a floor file.

mechanisms.problemSolved: An add-to-basket that does not confirm makes the buyer press it twice, and a filter that does not acknowledge makes them assume it is broken.

mechanisms.whyItWorks: 100ms is a perception threshold, not an aesthetic value, so it pins nothing visual. It sharpens SKILL.md:167-169's 'every interactive state exists' into three named commerce actions with a deadline.

mechanisms.problemSolved: A buyer who cannot see what they have accumulated stops accumulating.
mechanisms.mechanism: What the buyer has committed to so far, and how many, is visible and reachable from every surface including narrow viewports.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: It states the fact that must be visible rather than the component that shows it, which is what lets a header icon, a side rail and a plain text line all count.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Filters built from the warehouse's categories, an unstated result count, and an empty result that is a dead end.
mechanisms.mechanism: The buyer can narrow the set on the terms they think in, always knows how many results they are looking at, and is never given a dead end: an empty result offers the nearest thing that exists.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Three content obligations with no layout implied. The empty-result clause is the sharpest of them and is the commerce case of SKILL.md:167-169's 'empty state is an invitation'.
mechanisms.sitesmithForm: floor/buy.md, listing obligations. Drop 'a grid' (line 41) and 'sort is secondary to filter' (line 42) — a grid is one rendition and the sort ranking is not generally true.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Category trees that mirror how stock is organised rather than how buyers ask for things.
mechanisms.mechanism: Categories are named and grouped in the buyer's nouns, not the warehouse's.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: It is a naming and grouping obligation, orthogonal to how the structure is exposed — which is why the mega-menu prescription that follows it (145-147) is a separate thing and is appearance.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Card chrome, badges and framing that compete with the photograph of the thing being sold.
mechanisms.mechanism: On any surface where the object appears it is the largest and most legible thing there; chrome does not compete with it. This is the mode where imagery cannot be substituted.

mechanisms.problemSolved: A catalogue photographed inconsistently reads as a reseller's scrape, and a single angle hides what the buyer needs to see.
mechanisms.mechanism: The object is shown from more than one angle, treated identically across the whole catalogue, with detail views wherever the material is part of the purchase.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: Consistency-of-treatment is the obligation; which treatment is a direction decision, and three catalogues can be internally consistent while looking nothing like each other.

mechanisms.problemSolved: A photograph cannot convey size, and size is the most common cause of a return.
mechanisms.mechanism: Physical scale is established explicitly: dimensions, a hand, or a known object in frame.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: The source sentence supplies its own three unrelated renditions, which is the clearest proof in the file that it is an obligation rather than a look.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Generated product imagery that will not match the shipped catalogue, produced because an empty image slot looks unfinished.
mechanisms.mechanism: Where the real photograph does not exist yet, a labelled placeholder states the shot required — subject, crop, ground — and that is a legitimate finished answer.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Undifferentiated 'you may also like' rails that serve neither the buyer who is in the wrong place nor the buyer who is in the right one.

mechanisms.problemSolved: Irregular repeated units read as a rendering bug, and figures that shift under their own digits force the buyer to compare arithmetically instead of visually.
mechanisms.mechanism: Repeated units in a set are consistent enough, and compared figures aligned enough, that comparing two objects is a glance rather than a task.
mechanisms.whyItWorks: The obligation is comparability. Tabular figures are one rendition of it; decimal alignment and a one-object-per-screen layout that carries figures forward are two others that share no visual language with it.
